what_its_for: Sertraline is used to treat depression, anxiety, panic attacks, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). It belongs to a group of medicines called SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors), which work by increasing the level of serotonin, a natural chemical in your brain that helps improve your mood.
how_to_take: Take sertraline by mouth, with or without food. Taking it with food may help reduce stomach upset. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Try to take it at the same time every day to help you remember. If you are using the liquid (oral concentrate), mix the dose with 4 ounces (half a cup) of water, ginger ale, lemon-lime soda, lemonade, or orange juice right before taking it. Do not mix it ahead of time.
dosing: Your doctor will tell you exactly how much sertraline to take. Most adults start with 25 to 50 mg once a day. Your doctor may slowly increase your dose up to 200 mg per day if needed. Never change your dose or stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel better. Stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms like dizziness, nausea, or irritability.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and just take your next regular dose. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store sertraline tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the liquid concentrate stored at room temperature as well. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of any unused or expired medicine safely — ask your pharmacist about a drug take-back program near you.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking sertraline, as it can increase dizziness and drowsiness and may make your condition worse. Do not take sertraline if you have used a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) such as phenelzine, tranylcypromine, or linezolid in the past 14 days, as this combination can be life-threatening. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you, as it may cause dizziness or drowsiness. Avoid taking blood thinners like warfarin or aspirin without your doctor's guidance, as sertraline may increase bleeding risk. Do not take St. John's Wort, as combining it with sertraline can cause a dangerous reaction.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: thoughts of suicide or self-harm, new or worsening depression or anxiety, unusual changes in mood or behavior, high fever, agitation, fast heartbeat, muscle stiffness, or confusion (these may be signs of a rare but serious condition called serotonin syndrome), unusual bleeding or bruising, seizures, or an allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing. Contact your doctor if you notice any side effects that concern you, such as nausea, diarrhea, dry mouth, trouble sleeping, dizziness, or sexual side effects like decreased sex drive.
when_it_works: Sertraline does not work right away. Most people start to notice some improvement in sleep, appetite, or energy within 1 to 2 weeks. However, it may take 4 to 6 weeks or longer to feel the full benefit. It is important to keep taking it even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor.
special_populations: Children and Teenagers: Sertraline is approved for children aged 6 and older for OCD, but it should be used with caution. Children and teens may have an increased risk of suicidal thoughts, especially at the start of treatment. Parents and caregivers should watch closely for any changes in mood or behavior. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Taking sertraline during the last trimester of pregnancy may cause temporary withdrawal symptoms in the newborn. However, stopping your medication without guidance can also be harmful — your doctor will help you weigh the risks and benefits. Breastfeeding: Sertraline passes into breast milk in small amounts. Talk to your doctor if you are breastfeeding. Older Adults: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects such as dizziness and a low sodium level in the blood. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose. Liver Problems: If you have liver problems, your doctor may need to adjust your dose, as sertraline is processed by the liver.
